old: could not accept their kind invitation.
new: could not accept the honor of their invitation, and so on.
source: unable to accept the honour of their invitation, etc.
reason: Austen's 'etc.' mocks the formulaic note of regret by cutting it short; 'kind invitation' drops the joke and the formula ('the honour of').

old: from being considered the most forbidding, disagreeable man present
new: from having a most forbidding, disagreeable face
source: not all his large estate in Derbyshire could save him from having a most forbidding, disagreeable countenance
reason: The irony is that the man just judged handsomer than Bingley suddenly acquires a forbidding face once his manners offend; the candidate turns 'countenance' into a general judgment of the man and inflates 'a most' into a superlative ('the most ... present').

source: She is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt _me_
reason: Set-up/pay-off: Charlotte quotes the word back in 5.8 ('to be only just _tolerable_'), and the candidate keeps 'tolerable' there, so Darcy must say it here; 'passable' breaks the famous echo.

source: You have liked many a stupider person.
reason: Elizabeth's joke is about Jane liking everyone (continued in 4.6 'people in general'); narrowing 'person' to 'man' implies romantic attachments to previous men.

old: had not been designed to please anyone in particular
new: had not been calculated to please people in general
source: their behaviour at the assembly had not been calculated to please in general
reason: 'Not calculated to please in general' means their conduct was not such as would please most people; 'anyone in particular' reverses the scope and makes it sound as if they were pleasant generally.

old: They therefore felt entitled, in every respect, to think
new: They were therefore, in every respect, entitled to think
source: and were, therefore, in every respect entitled to think well of themselves and meanly of others
reason: Austen's narrator ironically asserts, in mock-logical form, that expensive schooling, fortune and overspending 'entitled' them to contempt; 'felt entitled' flattens the irony into a plain report of their attitude.

old: the freedom to enjoy a gentleman's life
new: the sporting rights of a manor
source: as he was now provided with a good house and the liberty of a manor
reason: 'The liberty of a manor' is the right to hunt and shoot over its land, the main amenity of owning an estate; the vague gloss loses why renting Netherfield might make buying an estate seem unnecessary.

old: have the courage to truly fall in love
new: have heart enough to truly fall in love
source: there are very few of us who have heart enough to be really in love without encouragement
reason: 'Heart enough' is chiefly about depth of feeling (few love strongly enough to persist unencouraged), not bravery; 'courage' narrows it to one reading that the source doesn't commit to.

old: they both prefer Vingt-un to Commerce
new: they both prefer the card game Vingt-un to Commerce
source: they both like Vingt-un better than Commerce
reason: Modern readers won't recognize the two names as card games, and the joke depends on it; a two-word in-line gloss is enough.

source: They always continue to grow sufficiently unlike afterwards to have their share of vexation
reason: Charlotte's cynicism is cool understatement: 'vexation' means annoyance, not misery. The inflation makes her view of marriage bleaker than the source.

old: if I don't take the offensive first
new: if I don't begin by being impertinent myself
source: if I do not begin by being impertinent myself, I shall soon grow afraid of him
reason: Elizabeth plans playful cheek, not aggression. 'Impertinent' is still clear today and is a key word for her manner that comes back later in the novel (Darcy admiring her 'impertinence').

old: as I am fond of good company
new: as I am fond of superior society
source: for I am fond of superior society
reason: Sir William's 'superior society' is about rank, and it is the point of his social climbing next to Darcy; 'good company' just means pleasant companions.

old: was entailed—in the absence of male heirs—to a distant relation
new: was entailed—legally bound to pass, in the absence of male heirs, to a distant relation
source: was entailed, in default of heirs male, on a distant relation
reason: This is the reader's first meeting with the entail, which drives the plot; most modern readers don't know the term, and a short in-line gloss removes the obstacle.

old: brought back all of Elizabeth's original dislike
new: let Elizabeth enjoy all her original dislike once more
source: restored Elizabeth to the enjoyment of all her original dislike
reason: The ironic 'enjoyment' of dislike (Elizabeth relishing her justified prejudice) is dropped, leaving flat narration.

old: as they all seem to be
source: how young ladies can have patience to be so very accomplished as they all are
reason: Added hedge: Bingley flatly asserts they all are accomplished, which is what provokes Caroline's 'All young ladies accomplished!' and his 'Yes, all of them, I think.'

old: she was needed for the baking
new: she was needed to help with the mince pies
source: I fancy she was wanted about the mince-pies
reason: Drops the concrete detail that makes Mrs. Bennet's jab specific (Charlotte doing kitchen work, set against 'I always keep servants').

old: a sturdy, well-developed girl of fifteen
new: a sturdy, well-grown girl of fifteen
source: Lydia was a stout, well-grown girl of fifteen
reason: 'Well-grown' refers to her size and height (she is 'the tallest', 2.25); 'well-developed' adds a modern sexualized implication that the source doesn't have.
